\title{Which Parts of BM25 Help Learned Top-$k$ Selection?\\
Tests in Sparse Retrieval, KV-Cache Page Selection and Expert Routing}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Learned sparse retrieval, KV-cache page selection and mixture-of-experts routing keep the
top $k$ items by a learned score. Lexical retrieval corrects its score with BM25's inverse
document frequency (IDF), saturation and length normalisation, and prior work attributes
BM25's gain on learned features to a Zipf-like feature-frequency curve. We evaluate fourteen sparse codes derived from one
frozen dense encoder under all eight on/off combinations of the three components on
thirteen collections. The full correction beats the plain inner product in 162 of the
182 code--collection pairs, but a predictor built from the frequency curve and fixed before
the experiment does no better than always predicting a gain. Exact Shapley values assign
$62\%$ of the gain to saturation, which uses only the document's own values, and tests
fixed in advance confirm that its effect follows the spread of the stored values. A rule that uses
agreement with text BM25 to decide, without relevance labels, whether IDF and length
normalisation help gets the sign right no more often than a constant guess on rows it had
not seen and on SPLADE-v3. In KV selection
and routing we take an item's frequency to be how often the selector chose it during
calibration. With IDF on, the selected KV pages hold $0.21$ to $0.44$ of full attention's
softmax mass, against $0.90$ to $0.95$ without. Mean RULER accuracy falls from $0.71$ and
$0.78$ (two token budgets) to at most $0.046$ on Qwen2.5-1.5B and, in a replication
registered before it ran, from $0.43$ and $0.46$ to at most $0.002$ on Llama-3.2-1B. Mean MMLU accuracy on OLMoE
falls from $0.480$ to at most $0.390$. The frequency-curve predictor is wrong in sign on every KV row
with a nonzero margin and on 52 of 55 MMLU subjects.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

In lexical retrieval, BM25 adjusts the raw term-count score in three ways. Inverse
document frequency (IDF) discounts features that occur throughout the collection,
saturation stops rewarding repeated evidence past a point, and length normalisation
adjusts for document length \citep{sparckjones1972idf,robertson2009bm25}. Three learned
selectors score without these corrections. A learned sparse retriever scores a query
against a document by an inner product over non-negative features and returns the top $k$
\citep{formal2021splade,nguyen2023unified}. Quest, a KV-cache sparsity method, scores
fixed-size pages of the key-value cache against the current query and attends only to the
highest-scoring pages \citep{tang2024quest}. A mixture-of-experts router scores every
expert and sends the token to the top $k$ \citep{shazeer2017moe,fedus2022switch}. Each
score is non-negative or can be made so, and BM25's correction can be applied to all three
(Figure~\ref{fig:overview}). In retrieval the score is a sum over many features. For a KV
page or an expert it is a single number, and saturation alone then cannot change the
selection (Proposition~\ref{prop:single}).

Each part of BM25 was designed for words. Applied to learned features, BM25 has both
helped and hurt. On one benchmark suite BM25 beats the inner product by $0.20$ nDCG@10 on
sparse-autoencoder features and loses by $0.11$ on SPLADE-v3 \citep{clavie2026latent}. The
explanation offered is that BM25 helps when the features' document frequencies follow a
Zipf-like curve, as word frequencies do \citep{clavie2026latent,han2026bm25v}. If that is
right, statistics of the frequency curve should predict the sign of the gain before the
experiment is run.

We tested this prediction in retrieval and in two other top-$k$ selections, and it failed
in all three. Each test was fixed in a dated commit before its predictions were computed, and
we call such tests registered (Table~\ref{tab:registered}). We derive fourteen sparse
representations from one frozen dense encoder, multilingual E5-base, and score each under
all eight combinations of the three components on thirteen collections. The correction
helped almost everywhere, but the registered frequency-curve predictor did not predict the size of the
gain. Most of the gain comes from saturation, a component that uses no collection
statistics, and the spread of the stored values predicts the size of its effect on
held-out parameter settings. Whether IDF and length normalisation help is harder to
predict, and a registered rule that decides this without relevance labels, from agreement with
text BM25, fails on SPLADE-v3. In KV selection and routing we take an item's frequency to be how often the
selector chose it during calibration. IDF then favours items the selector rarely chose, and
accuracy falls in both.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item A grid of fourteen representations under all eight configurations on thirteen
collections, $1{,}358$ rows, with an exact Shapley decomposition of the gain
(Section~\ref{sec:attribution}).
\item Six registered tests (Table~\ref{tab:registered}). The saturation hypotheses pass,
the frequency-curve predictor fails wherever it has a pass mark, and the label-free rule
fails on SPLADE-v3 with its registered reference, and fails in KV selection only because a
constant guess also scores perfectly there.
\item A mechanism for saturation's gain, confirmed by tests fixed in advance, and evidence that index
statistics predict it but not the gain from IDF and length normalisation
(Sections~\ref{sec:predicts} to~\ref{sec:splade}).
\item The correction in KV selection, on two models, and in routing, with a label-free
check by exact attention mass and a proof that, without IDF, saturation cannot change a
single-score selection (Sections~\ref{sec:problem} and~\ref{sec:transfer}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Term weighting and learned sparse retrieval.} IDF began as a statistical account
of term specificity \citep{sparckjones1972idf}. Saturation approximates the two-Poisson
model of within-document frequency \citep{robertson1994poisson}, and pivoted length
normalisation keeps long documents from being favoured or penalised
\citep{singhal1996pivoted}. BM25 combines the three \citep{robertson2009bm25}. Learned
sparse retrievers learn term weights and score by inner product, through contextual exact
match \citep{gao2021coil} or expansion over the subword vocabulary in SPLADE
\citep{formal2021splade,formal2021spladev2,lassance2024spladev3}.

\paragraph{BM25 on learned features.} Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense
activations into many non-negative features \citep{cunningham2024sae,gao2025topksae}.
\citet{clavie2026latent} score SAE features of a frozen dense retriever with BM25 and
report $0.582$ nDCG@10 against $0.381$ for the inner product, and the reverse on SPLADE-v3,
$0.455$ against $0.568$. CL-SR loses 11 to 18 percent of its nDCG@10 on TREC-DL without IDF
\citep{park2025clsr}. \citet{han2026bm25v} find BM25 and the inner product about equal on
image features and credit top-$k$ filtering for suppressing what IDF would down-weight.
None of these varies the representation systematically or separates all three components.

\paragraph{Predicting effectiveness without labels.} Query performance prediction estimates
retrieval quality from the query and the ranking
\citep{carmel2010difficulty,cronen2002clarity,shtok2012nqc}. Systems can be ranked without
judgements against pseudo-relevant documents from pooled output
\citep{soboroff2001ranking}. We apply the same idea to a new target, the
difference between two scorers.

\paragraph{Selection inside the transformer.} Quest scores KV pages against page min-max key
summaries \citep{tang2024quest}. H2O keeps recent tokens and heavy hitters, the tokens that
have received the most attention \citep{zhang2023h2o}, SnapKV the positions recent queries attend to
\citep{li2024snapkv}, StreamingLLM the first tokens and a recent window
\citep{xiao2024streamingllm}, and Expected Attention the positions future queries are
predicted to attend to \citep{devoto2025expectedattention}.
Mixture-of-experts layers route each token to its top-$k$ experts
\citep{shazeer2017moe,lepikhin2021gshard,fedus2022switch}, balanced by an auxiliary loss
\citep{zoph2022stmoe} or a load-driven bias \citep{wang2024lossfree}, whose analogue we run as
a baseline. We know of no work that applies BM25's components to KV selection or routing.

\section{Problem and Registered Tests}
\label{sec:problem}

\paragraph{The correction.} For query and document vectors $x_q, x_d$ with non-negative
coordinates we score
\begin{equation}
S(q,d) = \sum_{j} x_{qj}\, w_j\, T(x_{dj}, \ell_d).
\label{eq:scorer}
\end{equation}
The weight $w_j$ is one or $\idf_j = \ln(1 + (N - df_j + 0.5)/(df_j + 0.5))$, where feature
$j$ is nonzero in $df_j$ of the $N$ documents. The length factor $\ell_d$ is one or
$1 - b + b L_d/\overline{L}$, with $L_d = \sum_j x_{dj}$, $\overline{L}$ its mean over the
collection, and BM25 parameters $k_1$ and $b$. The transform $T(f,\ell)$ is $f/\ell$ or the
saturated $(k_1+1)f/(f + k_1\ell)$. Length normalisation without saturation divides each
value by $\ell_d$, a variant BM25 does not contain. Each component is on (1) or off (0),
and a configuration is written as three bits in the order IDF, saturation, length, so
\texttt{010} is saturation alone. Configuration \texttt{000} (all-off) is the plain inner
product and \texttt{111} (all-on) is BM25. IDF and length normalisation need collection
statistics (document frequencies and mean length), and saturation uses only the document's
own values.

\paragraph{Rows and targets.} One row pairs a representation with a collection at one
support budget (a cap on nonzero features), one pair $(k_1, b)$ and one basis seed, and
carries eight nDCG@10 values $Q_c$, one per configuration $c$. The 182 primary rows are the
fourteen representations on the thirteen collections at the default budget, parameters and
seed. The registered target is the margin $m = (Q_{111} - Q_{000})/\operatorname{sd}(Q_{000},
\ldots, Q_{111})$, the gain of BM25 over the inner product in units of the spread of the
eight scores. It is undefined in three primary rows where all eight scores are equal. The
Shapley value of component $s$ averages its marginal effect over every order in which the
components can be turned on \citep{shapley1953value}. Writing $Q_A$ for the configuration
with the components in $A$ on,
\begin{equation}
\phi_s = \sum_{A \not\ni s}
\tfrac{|A|!\,(2-|A|)!}{6}\bigl(Q_{A\cup\{s\}} - Q_{A}\bigr),
\label{eq:shapley}
\end{equation}
and the three values sum to $Q_{111} - Q_{000}$. The collection gain $G = Q_{111} - Q_{010}$
is the value of IDF and length normalisation once saturation is applied, and its sign
answers the practical question of whether to use collection statistics.

\paragraph{Predictors.} The frequency-curve predictor, planned in the proposal and fixed in code on 19
September before any retrieval run, is a ridge
regression of $m$ on three diagnostics of the feature-frequency curve (the Zipf slope, the variance of IDF and the
activation share of the most frequent $1\%$ of features). The label-free rule replaces
$Q_c$ by a pseudo-quality $\tilde{Q}_c$, the nDCG@10 of configuration $c$'s top 100 when
the top 10 of a reference ranker on the same query are taken as relevant. The registered
reference is text BM25, and the dense encoder and the two fused by reciprocal rank are
secondary. The substitution gives estimates $\tilde{\phi}_s$ and $\tilde{G}$ with no fitted
parameter, and the rule uses \texttt{111} where $\tilde{G} > 0$ and \texttt{010} otherwise.
A second, fitted predictor regresses $\phi_{\mathrm{idf}}$, $\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$,
$\phi_{\mathrm{len}}$ and $G$ on three nested tiers of features. The first holds the
pre-registered diagnostics. The second adds index statistics, which describe the nonzero
values stored in the index, chiefly their coefficient of variation $\mathrm{cv}_x$. The
third, the pseudo-label tier, adds the pseudo-qualities and features of each
configuration's top-100 ranking.

\paragraph{Transfer.} Eq.~\eqref{eq:scorer} applies to any selection with a non-negative
score and a frequency count. Each KV page $i$ in a head is one item with one stored value
$f_i$, so the sum in Eq.~\eqref{eq:scorer} has one term. The value is Quest's criticality,
an upper bound on the query--key product computed from the page's key minima and maxima,
passed through a softplus and divided by the head's median selected value during
calibration. Calibration runs Quest at 64 positions of the example's own prompt. The
page's document frequency is the number of these positions, among those at or after the
page, at which Quest selects it, and $N$ is the number of calibration positions at or after the page. The
page's length is the norm of its
concatenated key minima and maxima. For expert $e$ the value is the router probability,
the frequency is the share of calibration tokens routed to $e$, and the length is the norm
of the token's router logits, which all experts of a token share. The selected experts keep
their original gate weights. A row is one RULER task at one token budget in KV selection,
and WikiText or one MMLU subject in routing. The frequency-curve predictor fitted in
retrieval is applied without refitting.

\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:single}
When each item carries a single score $f_i \ge 0$, as a KV page or an expert does, and IDF
is off, the saturated score is a strictly increasing function of $f_i/\ell_i$ and selects
the same top $k$ as the unsaturated score, up to ties.
\end{proposition}

It holds because $(k_1+1)f/(f+k_1\ell) = g(f/\ell)$ with $g(f) = (k_1+1)f/(f+k_1)$, and $g$
is strictly increasing on $f \ge 0$. With IDF on, $\idf_i\,g(f_i)$ and $\idf_i f_i$ can
order items differently. In routing all experts of a token share one length, so dividing by
it does not change their order either. So the four configurations with IDF off route
identically up to ties, as do \texttt{100} and \texttt{101}.

\paragraph{Registration.} The tests in Table~\ref{tab:registered} come from the project
proposal (August), a hypotheses file (29 September), a registration file (20 October), and
an addendum (23 October), written after the Qwen results were read and before any Llama
run, that registered the Llama replication. Each was committed before the predictions it
tests were computed. The limit of $1.81$ on mean absolute error (MAE) is
$1.5$ times the frequency-curve predictor's RMSE on $m$ in retrieval with corpora held out ($1.21$).
Always predicting a gain is already right on $90\%$ of the 179 retrieval rows, so our
interim report (2 October) added, before any transfer run, the condition of beating that
majority sign. The better constant is whichever of always predicting a gain and always
predicting a loss is right more often on the rows tested, and the label-free rule must
exceed it. Always-on applies \texttt{111} in every row, \emph{never} applies saturation alone
(\texttt{010}) in every row, and the oracle picks the better of the two in each row.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Representations.} All representations come from \texttt{multilingual-e5-base}
(E5, \citealp{wang2024me5}) at a pinned revision. Seven bases map an E5 state to a
non-negative sparse vector, those that need fitting on the same $200{,}000$ MS~MARCO
passages \citep{bajaj2016msmarco}. They are the identity, a Gaussian projection to 768 dimensions and PCA to 384, each
split into positive and negative parts; soft $k$-means over $4{,}096$ centroids; product
and residual quantisation ($8 \times 256$, \citealp{jegou2011pq,chen2010rq}); and a
Top-$K$ SAE with $8{,}192$ features of which at most 32 are active. They form four basis
families for held-out validation (linear, clustered, quantised and learned). Pooled
granularity applies a basis to the mean of the token states, and token granularity applies
it to each state before summing, so seven bases at two granularities give fourteen
representations. In the primary budget the support, the number of nonzero features, is
capped at 32 per query and 128 per document, and document frequencies, lengths and IDF come
from the capped vectors of each corpus. Retrieval is exact over the whole corpus with
$k_1 = 1.2$ and $b = 0.75$.

\paragraph{Collections and sweeps.} The thirteen collections come from eleven corpora:
MS~MARCO dev with TREC-DL 2019 and 2020 on the same documents, six BEIR sets
\citep{thakur2021beir}, LIMIT \citep{weller2025limit} and the Hindi, Bengali and Telugu
portions of MIRACL \citep{zhang2023miracl}. Beyond the primary rows, sweeps vary one
setting each (Table~\ref{tab:families} in the appendix). SPLADE-v3
\citep{lassance2024spladev3}, with its own backbone, is scored under the same eight
configurations as an external comparison.

\paragraph{Significance.} All-on is compared with all-off by a paired bootstrap over
queries or examples ($10{,}000$ draws; $2{,}000$ for SPLADE-v3 and the transfer settings)
that recomputes both parts of $m$, with Holm's correction for multiple comparisons within
each pre-declared group of rows \citep{holm1979}.

\paragraph{KV-page selection.} The attention model is Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct
\citep{qwen2025qwen25} in float16, chosen before any run, and
Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct is run with the same protocol as a replication registered before it
started. All thirteen tasks of the RULER long-context benchmark \citep{hsieh2024ruler},
from needle retrieval to QA, are run at a 4K context with 100 examples per task and token
budgets of 512 and 1{,}024 over sixteen-token pages. Prefill is dense and decoding attends
only to the selected pages. Full attention, Quest and H2O \citep{zhang2023h2o} are run
beside the eight configurations, and \texttt{000} reproduces Quest's output on every
example. The label-free reference is exact attention mass, the share of full-attention
softmax mass that falls on the pages a configuration would select, measured along the
full-attention generation.

\paragraph{Expert routing.} OLMoE-1B-7B \citep{muennighoff2025olmoe} routes each token to 8
of 64 experts. Quality is the mean token log-likelihood on WikiText-2
\citep{merity2017wikitext} in 2{,}048-token windows, reported as perplexity, and zero-shot
accuracy on each of the 57 MMLU subjects \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu}, scored by the
likelihood of each choice. Frequencies come from 256 training-split windows for WikiText
and from each subject's own prompts for MMLU. A load-driven frequency bias, the analogue of
loss-free balancing \citep{wang2024lossfree}, is run beside the eight configurations.

\section{Results in Retrieval}
\label{sec:retrieval}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{5pt}
\input{tables/tab_quality}
\caption{nDCG@10 of text BM25 and of E5, the dense encoder the codes come from; the mean over
the fourteen codes under \texttt{000} and \texttt{111}; the best single code under
\texttt{111}; and SPLADE-v3 under both. MIRACL is outside SPLADE-v3's vocabulary.}
\label{tab:quality}
\end{table*}

\subsection{The correction helps the E5 codes}

Under the inner product the mean nDCG@10 of the sparse codes, capped at 32 and 128
features, is at most $0.135$ on every collection (Table~\ref{tab:quality}). The full
correction raises their mean on every collection. Per row, all-on beats all-off in 162 of
the 179 primary rows where $m$ is defined ($90\%$), and significantly after Holm correction
in 134 of all 182. Under all-on the best code (the token-level SAE on twelve of the
thirteen collections) beats text BM25 on six. Yet all-on is the strict best of
the eight configurations in only 42 of the 182 rows, and the mean of \texttt{011}
(saturation and length without IDF, $0.163$) is above that of \texttt{111} ($0.158$). The
inner product scores below $0.01$ in 81 rows, so nearly any correction beats it.

\subsection{The frequency-curve predictor predicts almost nothing}

The frequency-curve predictor explains almost none of the held-out variance of $m$, with $R^2$ of
$0.04$ when a basis family is held out and $0.02$ when a corpus is held out, and its sign
accuracy equals that of always predicting a gain. Part of the failure lies in the target.
Of the margins, $85\%$ fall between $1.5$ and $3.5$, because in many rows $Q_{000}$ is near
zero and every other configuration is far above it, so $m$ reflects that pattern more than
the size of the gain.

\subsection{Where the gain comes from}
\label{sec:attribution}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.4pt}
\input{tables/tab_shapley}
\caption{Mean Shapley value of each component (Eq.~\ref{eq:shapley}) and their sum
$Q_{111} - Q_{000}$, in each setting's metric (nDCG@10 in retrieval, accuracy in KV
selection and MMLU, log-likelihood per token on WikiText). 16/64 and 64/256 are the
query and document support caps of the other budgets, and native is uncapped.}
\label{tab:shapley}
\end{table}

Saturation has the largest Shapley value at every support budget (Table~\ref{tab:shapley}).
Over the 182 primary rows it takes $62\%$ of the gain, length normalisation $28\%$ and IDF
$10\%$, so collection statistics account for $38\%$ ($95\%$ interval $36$ to $41\%$,
resampling collections). IDF, the component the Zipfian account is about, contributes
least. As supports grow, the share of IDF shrinks and that of length grows, and with
uncapped (native) supports IDF's mean Shapley value is slightly negative.
\citet{han2026bm25v} report the same trend for image features, where document frequencies
converge as more features are active. IDF's small gain does depend on the real
frequencies. On ArguAna, NFCorpus and SciFact, shuffling them turns IDF's mean Shapley
value negative, and the real value is larger in $83\%$ of the 42 rows (one-sided Wilcoxon
$p < 10^{-6}$). Removing IDF altogether, by making all frequencies equal, does not lower
all-on nDCG@10 there ($0.157$ without against $0.147$ with, $p = 0.15$).

\subsection{What the index predicts}
\label{sec:predicts}

The spread of the stored values ($\mathrm{cv}_x$) predicts saturation's Shapley value. With length
normalisation off, saturation maps a stored value $f$ to $g(f)$, and $g(f)/f$ falls as $f$
grows. If every stored value in the index were equal, $g$ would rescale every score by one
factor and the ranking would not move. Pooled PQ and RQ are such codes, and their
saturation and length effects are exactly zero in every row (Table~\ref{tab:bases} in the
appendix). The more unequal the values, the more saturation can reorder a ranking for a
given $k_1$ and set of queries. In our codes that reordering usually helps
($\phi_{\mathrm{sat}} > 0$ in $79\%$ of primary rows). We committed six hypotheses on this mechanism before running them on
the $k_1$ and $b$ sweep of five collections, rows not used when the hypotheses were formed
(Table~\ref{tab:confirm} in the appendix). All six pass. H5 (no length effect at $b = 0$)
is a code check, and H1 overlaps the primary rows. H2, H3, H4 and H6 test the mechanism. In
H4 a ridge model of $\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$ on $\mathrm{cv}_x$ fitted at $k_1 = 1.2$ ranks
$\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$ at $k_1 = 0.6$ and $2.4$ with Spearman $0.87$ and $0.90$.

IDF and length normalisation also move the ranking by an amount the index fixes. Whether
those moves help depends on whether long documents were over-rewarded and whether rare
features separate relevant documents from the rest. For the strongest codes, token-level
SAE and token-level PCA, $G > 0$ on fewer than half the collections. Index statistics
predict little of $G$ (held-out $R^2$ of $0.01$ to $0.12$, Table~\ref{tab:predictor} in the
appendix). We take relevance to be the missing input (Section~\ref{sec:proxy}).

\subsection{Supplying relevance without labels}
\label{sec:proxy}

If what the index lacks is relevance, a proxy for relevance should restore the
prediction. Only the pseudo-label tier reaches positive held-out $R^2$ on every
target and held-out split, and for $G$ it reaches $0.44$ to $0.59$, against at most $0.13$
without pseudo-labels (Table~\ref{tab:predictor}). Within a row the pseudo-quality orders the eight
configurations almost as $Q_c$ does (median Spearman $0.98$). The rule was designed on the
primary rows. On the 181 whose features are all defined, it raises mean nDCG@10 from $0.159$ (always-on) to $0.163$. The oracle reaches $0.165$, so
the rule recovers $59\%$ of the difference.

With the BM25 reference of the interim rule, its sign on rows it had not seen is no better
than a constant. The interim report
fixed the rule before the 84 rows at the two other support budgets on the three MS~MARCO
collections were produced. On those rows $\tilde{G}$ and $G$ have Spearman $0.91$ with the
BM25 reference, but the sign is right on $0.87$ of rows, against $0.88$ for always
predicting a gain. With the dense or fused reference it is right on $0.95$, but the dense
reference is the encoder the codes come from. Always-on
scores $0.202$ and the oracle $0.203$, so at most $0.001$ can be gained. The three
collections share one corpus, so these rows are not independent.

\section{The Correction on SPLADE-v3}
\label{sec:splade}

SPLADE-v3 under the inner product averages $0.523$ nDCG@10, and the correction lowers it
on 8 of 10 collections and lowers the mean to $0.509$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality}). All-on is significantly worse
on four collections and significantly better on ArguAna and LIMIT (bootstrap $p < 0.05$,
uncorrected). The direction matches the reversal of \citet{clavie2026latent}; the size,
$0.013$ against their $0.113$, does not. Inside BM25, length normalisation costs $0.019$
($0.528$ for \texttt{110} against $0.509$ for \texttt{111}). Its Shapley value, $-0.073$
(Table~\ref{tab:shapley}), is larger because it also averages over \texttt{001} and
\texttt{101}, which divide by length without saturation and score $0.13$ and $0.12$ below
\texttt{000} and \texttt{100} respectively. Saturation's Shapley value of $0.048$ comes from adding it to
those two configurations. Added to \texttt{000} or \texttt{100}, it changes mean nDCG@10 by
less than $0.01$.

Here the sign of $G$ splits five to five, so a constant sign scores only $0.50$. With the
registered BM25 reference the label-free rule fails. $\tilde{G}$ has the right sign on five
of ten collections and correlates with $G$ at $-0.04$. On the three MS~MARCO collections,
adding IDF and length normalisation raises agreement with BM25 by $0.06$ to $0.08$ while
lowering nDCG@10. Agreement with BM25 is higher for configurations that behave like BM25,
the bias the registration named in advance. The secondary dense reference meets both
marks. Its sign is right on 7 of 10 collections, and its rule scores $0.519$, against
$0.509$ for always-on and $0.515$ for \emph{never}. Over ten collections the $95\%$ interval for the
gain over always-on includes zero. The fused reference fails.

\section{Transfer to KV Pages and Experts}
\label{sec:transfer}

\subsection{KV-page selection}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.5pt}
\input{tables/tab_attention}
\caption{Mean RULER accuracy (13 tasks, 4K context, 100 examples each) and mean share of
full attention's softmax mass on the pages each configuration would select, at token
budgets of 512 and 1{,}024. Full is full attention, and Quest equals \texttt{000} on every
example. Llama's mass excludes the first single-needle task, where full attention gives an
empty answer.}
\label{tab:attention}
\end{table*}

On Qwen, variable tracking scores zero under every configuration and under full attention
(see the limitations), so its two rows have no defined margin. With IDF on, mean accuracy on Qwen
falls to $0.015$ to $0.046$, against $0.71$ and $0.78$ for Quest at the two budgets, and
the configurations without IDF stay within $0.02$ of Quest (Table~\ref{tab:attention}).
After Holm correction all-on is significantly worse than all-off in all 24 remaining rows
and better in none, and $G$ is negative in all 24. The mean Shapley value of IDF is
$-0.775$, against $-0.003$ for saturation and $0.002$ for length (Table~\ref{tab:shapley}).

The registered replication on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct shows the same pattern. With IDF on,
mean accuracy is at most $0.002$, against $0.43$ and $0.46$ for Quest. After Holm
correction all-on is significantly worse than all-off in 18 of the 23 rows with a defined
margin and better in none, and IDF's mean Shapley value is $-0.509$. The three undefined
rows, where all eight configurations score zero, are both budgets of the first
single-needle task and variable tracking at the larger budget.

With IDF on, the selection moves to pages that hold on average less than half of the attention mass. A page's
frequency, as we defined it, is Quest's own selection rate during calibration, so IDF
down-weights the pages Quest selected most often, and the outcome is partly fixed by this
definition. A page selected at all 64 calibration positions gets the smoothed IDF
$\ln(1 + 0.5/64.5) \approx 0.008$ and one never selected gets $\ln 130 \approx 4.9$. On the
first single-needle task with Qwen at the 1{,}024 budget, the page holding the needle ranks
between second and tenth of 210 to 247 pages by selection rate, so IDF gives it one of the
lowest weights. Exact attention mass shows this on every task. Averaged over tasks, the
pages a configuration with IDF on would select hold $0.29$ to $0.44$ of the softmax mass on
Qwen and $0.21$ to $0.32$ on Llama, against $0.90$ to $0.95$ without IDF, and on every task
each configuration with IDF on holds less mass than any without.

As Proposition~\ref{prop:single} predicts, saturation without IDF changes the task score
almost nowhere. On Qwen, \texttt{010} and \texttt{000} differ in task score on 38 of
$2{,}600$ example--budget pairs and in output on at least 448. We attribute both to float16 ties.

The registered frequency-curve predictor fails on both models. On Qwen it predicts a gain
on all 24 rows and is wrong on every one, with an MAE of $4.18$ against the limit of
$1.81$. On Llama it is wrong on every row with a nonzero margin, with an MAE of $4.00$. Its
predictions on Qwen range only from $2.13$ to $2.21$. It predicts a gain for nearly any
input, so this failure says little about page frequency.

The registered label-free rule uses exact attention mass as its reference. Since IDF's pages
always hold less mass, $\tilde{G} < 0$ on every row where the reference exists (26 on Qwen, 24 on Llama). On the rows with $G
\ne 0$ (24 and 22) its sign is always right, and the retrieval majority sign is never
right. The configurations it picks reach the oracle's mean accuracy ($0.742$ over the 26
Qwen rows, $0.484$ over the 24 Llama rows with a reference), against $0.024$ and $0.001$ for always-on. It still fails the registered
test. With no row having $G > 0$, always predicting a loss also scores $1.00$, and the pass
mark requires exceeding it. We did not foresee this for Qwen, and the Llama addendum stated
it in advance. Across rows, $\tilde{G}$ and $G$ have Spearman $-0.32$ on Qwen and $-0.03$ on
Llama, so the rule gets the direction but not the size. Output agreement with full
attention, the secondary reference, gives the same decisions.

\subsection{Expert routing}


Configuration \texttt{000} is the native forward pass. As Section~\ref{sec:problem}
predicts, \texttt{001} to \texttt{011} give the same result as \texttt{000} on every
example, and \texttt{101} the same as \texttt{100} (Table~\ref{tab:routing} in the appendix). With IDF on, mean MMLU
accuracy falls from $0.480$ to between $0.382$ and $0.390$, and WikiText perplexity rises
from $7.49$ to $7.86$ and $7.88$. All-on is worse than all-off on 52 subjects and better on
3, and significantly worse after Holm correction in 22 of the 58 rows (57 subjects and
WikiText). As in KV selection, an expert's frequency is the router's own selection rate
during calibration, so IDF sends tokens towards experts the router rarely chooses. The
frequency bias, which adds a load-balancing term to the router probability instead of
multiplying it, loses less (MMLU $0.428$, perplexity $7.73$). The frequency-curve predictor gives
$2.05$ to $2.18$ for every subject, and its sign is right on 3 of the 55 subjects with a
nonzero margin ($0.05$), with an MAE of $3.98$ against the limit of $1.81$. It is also wrong
in sign on WikiText. No label-free rule was registered for routing, because its planned
reference, the output of a mixture over all 64 experts, was not implemented.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Index statistics predict little of $G$ in our data, and the label-free rule depends on
its reference. Agreement with BM25 is higher for configurations that behave like BM25, so on
SPLADE-v3 it favours the wrong ones. Exact attention mass picks the right setting on
every KV row with a reference, but so does a constant, and $\tilde{G}$ does not track the
size of $G$ (Spearman $-0.32$ on Qwen and $-0.03$ on Llama).

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

BM25's correction helps the E5 sparse codes mostly through saturation, whose effect
follows the spread of the stored values, and hurts SPLADE-v3 mostly through length
normalisation. The frequency curve does not predict whether collection statistics help.
Agreement with BM25 explains about half of the held-out variance of $G$, but as an unfitted
rule its sign is no better than a constant on new rows. With frequency taken as the selector's own selection
rate, IDF moves KV selection to pages holding on average $0.21$ to $0.44$ of the attention mass and lowers accuracy in
KV selection on two models and in expert routing.

\section*{Challenges, Limitations and Future Work}
\label{sec:limitations}

One encoder underlies every retrieval code, E5 saw MIRACL in training, and SPLADE is one
model. The KV runs use one 4K context and 100 examples per task, not the
planned 500. Variable tracking lacks
RULER's answer prefix and scores about zero in every configuration. Llama's full-attention answer is empty on the 100 first single-needle examples
and 262 others, mostly QA and multi-key, so its mass reference covers 938 of $1{,}300$. The label-free sign mark cannot be met when no
row has $G > 0$. Routing uses one model. A frequency counted over unrelated prompts is the next test.
